title.full: ASEAN Green Future Project Phase 2.1 & 2.2 Report, Decarbonizing the Philippine Power Sector

publisher.full: Sustainable Development Solutions Network and ClimateWorks Centre

description: Normative PH RE-nuclear pathway minimizing cost excl. externalities; near-zero power by 2060.
pathwayDescription:
Normative RE-nuclear pathway for the Philippine power sector aiming at near-zero emissions by 2060, with the same ambitious policy package and nuclear additions as MAP1 but optimised on cost alone, without pricing GHG externalities. More coal stays in the mix, so interim emissions are higher: power emissions reach 23.3 MtCO2e in 2050 versus 3.2 in MAP1. Cumulative investment is about USD 420bn by 2050, slightly below MAP1.

The ASEAN Green Future regional research project is run by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network, Climateworks Centre, and local researchers from leading universities. The project develops national policy analysis and near-zero pathways that are meant to provide policy recommendations and support policy makers.

coreDrivers.policies: MAP imposes accelerated fossil retirement, no new coal/gas beyond committed projects, higher offshore-wind deployment and RE-share targets; the pathway also adds nuclear capacity.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Normative pathway designed for near-zero power-sector emissions by 2060, with no explicit annual cap. The RE-nuclear system reaches it without GHG social costs in the objective, so interim emissions are higher than MAP1's (23.3 vs 3.2 MtCO2e in 2050).
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Least-cost optimization makes technology capital/O&M/fuel costs a core driver. MAP3 excludes monetized GHG externalities from the objective, allowing more coal use and higher interim emissions than its paired externality case.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Total cumulative investment in the power sector reaches USD 420bn by 2050, but no low carbon breakdown is provided. This is slightly less important than in MAP1.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Electricity demand is driven by common macro assumptions. Population follows the UN World Population Prospects 2019 medium-fertility projection.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Excluding environmental externalities from the objective is a distinctive scenario-design driver; the resulting system uses more coal and produces higher interim emissions than the paired externality-inclusive pathway.

dependencies.dependency_description: Critical (Explicit): The ambitious-policy package is a necessary design condition for the RE-nuclear outcome which includes accelerated fossil retirement, no new coal/gas beyond commitments, RE-share floors and 50 GW offshore wind by 2050, plus scheduled nuclear additions.

High (Explicit): The RE-nuclear pathway requires accelerated private fossil-asset retirement plus a nuclear legal/safety framework that the report says is still pending, making regulation a major feasibility condition.

High (Quantitative proxy): MAP3 requires US$642.8bn cumulative generation investment and 17.08 US¢/kWh generation cost by 2060, excluding externalities lowers interim cost but does not remove the financing/affordability constraint.
High (Explicit): The RE-nuclear pathway relies heavily on nuclear by mid-century, so unresolved public concerns about accidents, spent fuel and the Bataan legacy are a major enabling condition.

High (Quantitative proxy): MAP3 avoids charging environmental externalities in the objective but its 2050 generation cost remains about 17.29 US¢/kWh. Consumers therefore face nearly the same affordability burden as MAP1 while interim emissions are much higher.
High (Quantitative proxy): MAP3 delays part of the RE-nuclear build (86.2 GW in 2040) shifting rather than removing the grid/storage build requirement.

Moderate (Scenario-design inference): MAP3 uses the same RE-nuclear technology set as MAP1 but, without externalities, delays some low-carbon build and has lower capacity through 2040, slightly easing near-term technology-scaling pressure.

Moderate (Quantitative proxy): MAP3 relies on the same domestic RE resource base as MAP1 but its lower early low-carbon build reduces near-term pressure on wind/solar bounds. Resource needs converge later as the RE-nuclear systems converge.
The scenario provide social costs of environmental damage caused by GHG emissions but did not include it in its optimization model to diminish system costs.
